Predicting moiré magnetism with first-principles AI

Max Geier Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA    Liang Fu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
September 21, 2026
Abstract

Computational discovery of magnetic materials remains challenging because magnetism arises from the competition between kinetic energy and Coulomb interaction that is often beyond the reach of standard electronic-structure methods. Here we tackle this challenge by directly solving the many-electron Schrödinger equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo, which provides a highly expressive variational wavefunction for strongly correlated systems. Applying this technique to transition metal dichalcogenide moiré semicondutors, we predict itinerant ferromagnetism in WSe2/WS2 and an antiferromagnetic insulator in twisted Γ\Gamma-valley homobilayer, using the same neural network without any physics input beyond the microscopic Hamiltonian. Crucially, both types of magnetic states are obtained from a single calculation within the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector, removing the need to compute and compare multiple SzS_{z} sectors. This significantly reduces computational cost and paves the way for faster and more reliable magnetic material design.

Introduction.— Magnets play a key role in modern technology – powering permanent-magnet motors in vehicles, turbines, and robots, and enabling magnetic data storage and emerging spintronic functionality. Today’s highest-performance permanent magnets, NdFeB and SmCo, rely on rare-earth elements, whose limited availability motivates the search for rare-earth-free alternatives and new design principles. At a fundamental level, magnetism is intrinsically quantum: a classical many-particle system in equilibrium has zero magnetization even in the presence of an external magnetic field [9, 69, 70]. Instead, magnetism largely arises from long-range order of electron’s spin, driven by spin-independent Coulomb repulsion and kinetic energy – whereas direct magnetic dipole–dipole couplings are usually negligible [72].

The energy scale of magnetic ordering—as indicated by the Curie or Néel temperature—is typically much smaller than the Coulomb and kinetic energy scale. In metals, ferromagnetic ordering depends on the delicate balance between kinetic and interaction energies, and is often strongly influenced by exchange–correlation effects. In antiferromagnetic insulators, the ordering is often controlled by small kinetic‑exchange (superexchange) couplings arising from virtual hopping between localized orbitals. As a result, it is difficult to predict magnetism reliably by solving many-electron Schrödinger equation with standard electronic‑structure methods such as density functional theory or Hartree-Fock theory. As a paradigmatic example, it remains debated whether the uniform electron gas exhibits a ferromagnetic metal phase [16, 64].

Recently, neural networks have emerged as a powerful tool for constructing many-electron variational wavefunctions in continuous space [57, 34, 12, 73, 56]. Importantly, unlike handcrafted trial wavefunctions that are task specific, a single neural network with a large number of trainable parameters can accurately find a vast variety of ground states—including metallic, insulating, superconducting and topologically ordered states—purely through unsupervised energy minimization [27, 68, 40, 26, 2, 1], without pre-knowledge or physics-informed initialization. Moreover, certain fermionic network architectures have been mathematically proven to be universal, that is, capable of approximating any continuous wavefunctions to arbitrary accuracy at sufficient network size [23, 24]. Neural-network variational Monte Carlo studies have achieved impressive success on several correlated electron systems in real materials [42, 10, 45, 44, 41, 43, 46, 55].

In this work, we develop a neural-network variational Monte Carlo (NN-VMC) method to predict magnetism from first-principles by solving the many-electron Schrödinger equation directly. By allowing for general spin dependence in the wavefunction Ψ⁡(𝐫1,σ1,…,𝐫N,σN)\Psi({\bf r}_{1},\sigma_{1},...,{\bf r}_{N},\sigma_{N}), our fermionic network is capable of solving non-magnetic, ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic ground states on equal footing in S​U​(2)SU(2)-spin rotation invariant systems [7]. Our method eliminates the need of solving separately and comparing states of different magnetization, thus reducing the computational cost and attaining high accuracy.

We apply our first-principles neural-network method to study magnetism in two-dimensional Coulomb electron gas with a long-wavelength periodic potential. Such system is naturally realized in semiconductor moiré heterostructures such as WSe2/WS2 and twisted Γ\Gamma-valley homobilayers such as WS2, MoS2, MoSe2 [6, 78]. Our unbiased calculations predict metallic ferromagnet in the heterobilayer WSe2/WS2 and insulating antiferromagnet phases in homobilayers, depending on the filling factor.

Identifying magnetism.— For a SU(2)-symmetric electronic Hamiltonian, the spin operators commute with the Hamiltonian [H^,𝑺^2]=[H^,S^z]=0[\hat{H},{\hat{\bm{S}}}^{2}]=[\hat{H},\hat{S}_{z}]=0, so that eigenstates can be labeled by total spin S2=⟨𝑺^2⟩S^{2}=\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle and its component SzS_{z} along the zz direction. As a consequence, any ground state with total magnetization S>0S>0 appears as an (2​S+1)(2S+1)-fold degenerate multiplet with identical energy for all SzS_{z} sectors with |Sz|≤S|S_{z}|\leq S. This provides a direct, symmetry-based definition of magnetism: A system has a ferromagnetic ground state if it has total magnetization ⟨𝑺^2⟩>0\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle>0, which manifests as a degeneracy and equal total spin SS observed across as all sectors with |Sz|≤S|S_{z}|\leq S 11 1 We emphasize that also a state with magnetization smaller than the theoretical maximum of full polarization of all electrons ⟨𝑺^2⟩≤N2​(N2+1)\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle\leq\frac{N}{2}(\frac{N}{2}+1) is an ordinary ferromagnet. In fact this is the typical case; for example the core electrons usually do no participate in the ferromagnetic order..

Importantly, all possible total magnetization states ⟨𝑺^2⟩∈[0,N2​(N2+1)]\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle\in\left[0,\frac{N}{2}\left(\frac{N}{2}+1\right)\right], where NN is the number of electrons, can be realized in the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector. Therefore, solving for the lowest-energy in the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector identifies the ground state independent on its total magnetization ⟨𝑺^2⟩\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle. Practically however, reaching a finite magnetization ⟨𝑺^2⟩>0\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle>0 in the Sz=0S_{z}=0 requires that the numerical method is capable to express and reach a finite in-plane magnetization. Representing such spin-states is challenging for traditional numerical methods, and it is not a priori clear whether a variational numerical technique can efficiently represent and autonomously identify such states. Remarkably, our results below show that the NN-VMC technique identifies the fully spin-polarized state ⟨𝑺^2⟩=S⁡(S+1)​ℏ2\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle=S(S+1)\,\hbar^{2} already within the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector purely by energy minimization. This demonstrates that the approach is sufficiently expressive to identify magnetism from a single calculation at Sz=0S_{z}=0.

Neural Network Wavefunction and Variational Monte Carlo.— We employ a neural-network parameterization of the many-electron wavefunction within variational Monte Carlo to solve the continuum Schrödinger equation by direct energy minimization. The wavefunction is represented as a sum of KK determinants of generalized orbitals,

Ψ⁡(𝒙1,…,𝒙N)=∑k=1Kdeti​j​ϕjk​(𝒙i,𝒙/i),\Psi(\bm{x}_{1},…,\bm{x}_{N})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\det_{ij}\phi_{j}^{k}(\bm{x}_{i},{\bm{x}_{/i}}), (1)

where 𝒙i=(𝒓i,σi)\bm{x}_{i}=(\bm{r}_{i},\sigma_{i}) denotes the position 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} and spin σi\sigma_{i} of electron ii. The generalized orbitals ϕjk​(𝒙i,𝒙/i)\phi_{j}^{k}(\bm{x}_{i};{\bm{x}_{/i}}) explicitly encode many-body correlations by allowing the orbital of electron ii to depend on the configuration of all other electrons. The key advantage of this approach is that Eq. (1) yields a flexible amplitude and nodal structure which can universally represent two-dimensional fermionic wavefunctions using only a few determinants [23, 24]. Notably, the joint embedding of electron coordinate and spin—treated on equal footing—allows for spinful generalized orbitals in general form [7]. These orbitals in Eq. (1) are constructed using a transformer neural network, which is a universal approximator of permutation-equivariant sequence-to-sequence ({𝒙i}→{ϕj}\{\bm{x}_{i}\}\rightarrow\{\phi_{j}\}) functions [75]. The detailed construction of the neural network wavefunction is contained in Refs. [73, 27].

We employ Markov-chain Monte-Carlo sampling [21] for the efficient numerical evaluation of energy expectation values and observables. We employ employ a Kronecker factored curvature approximation [47] in the gradient updates, which leads to faster and more stable convergence [57, 11, 30]. Hyperparameters and training details are summarized in the Supplementary Material. A detailed description of the variational Monte Carlo technique is contained in Refs. [21, 57, 27] and peculiarities to spinful systems are discussed in Refs. [62, 4, 48, 49, 3, 29, 46, 41, 76, 7].

System.— In this work, we explore magnetism in two-dimensional semiconductor moiré materials. The first system of our study is doped WSe2/WS2, described by a continuum Hamiltonian [74, 79]:

H\displaystyle H =∑i(−ℏ22​m∗​∇i2+V⁡(𝐫i))+12​∑i∑i≠je24​π​ϵ​ϵ0​|𝐫i−𝐫j|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\left(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m^{*}}\nabla_{i}^{2}+V(\mathbf{r}_{i})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon\epsilon_{0}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|}, (2)

where V(𝐫)=−2V∑j=13cos⁡(𝐠j⋅𝐫+φ)V(\mathbf{r})=-2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\cos(\mathbf{g}_j \cdot\mathbf{r} + \varphi) is the moiré potential with reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐠j=4​π3​aM​(cos⁡2​π​j3,sin⁡2​π​j3)\mathbf{g}_{j}=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}a_{M}}(\cos\frac{2\pi j}{3},\sin\frac{2\pi j}{3}), moiré lattice constant aMa_{M}, and φ\varphi controls the shape of the moiré potential. This continuum Hamiltonian describes interacting electrons in a long-wavelength periodic potential arising from the moiré superlattice. A wide variety of emergent quantum phases has been studied in this moiré platform [61, 66, 36, 77, 60, 53], including Mott insulators, generalized Wigner crystals, and electron stripes.

So far metallic ferromagnetism has been theoretically predicted and experimentally observed in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) [14, 5], which hosts a pair of Chern bands with opposite Chern numbers for sz=±1/2s_{z}=\pm 1/2 electrons. In contrast, the continuum Hamiltonian (2) for WSe2/WS2 and similar TMD heterobilayers does not support topological bands and exhibits S​U​(2)SU(2) spin symmetry. For this class of moiré semiconductors, previous studies [15, 13, 50, 39, 63, 54, 59] have proposed kinetic mechanism for itinerant ferromagnetism based on a simplified Hubbard model description. However, a quantitatively accurate prediction from solving the first-principles interacting Hamiltonian has been lacking.

We search for itinerant magnetism in WSe2/WS2 bilayers using model parameters extracted from large-scale DFT calculations: effective mass m∗=0.5​mem^{*}=0.5\ m_{e}, moiré lattice constant aM=8.2​nma_{\rm M}=8.2\ {\rm nm}, moiré potential strength V=15​meVV=15\ {\rm meV}, shape φ=π/4\varphi=\pi/4, and dielectric constant of the surrounding hBN insulator ϵ=6\epsilon=6 [79].

Itinerant magnetism.— The typical interaction strength e24​π​ϵ​ϵ0​ℓ=56.9​meV\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon\epsilon_{0}\ell}=56.9\ {\rm meV} is large compared to the band width of the lowest energy band of 6.5​meV6.5\ {\rm meV} as well as the spacing to the next excited bands of 18​meV18\ {\rm meV} [Fig. 1(b)]. Here the length scale ℓ=aM/2​π/3=4.31​nm\ell=a_{\rm M}/\sqrt{2\pi/\sqrt{3}}=4.31\ {\rm nm} is average interparticle distance at density close to one electron per unit cell. Therefore both electron-correlation effects and interaction-induced mixing between bands are strong. As a consequence, this realistic system is not amenable to standard numerical treatments, which typically rely on projection of the full Hamiltonian to the lowest-energy band. In contrast, our first-principles neural network method operates directly in continuum real-space and thereby fully captures interaction-induced band-mixing – which is important for quantitatively accurate predictions.

As evidence of the magnetized ground state, we solve by direct energy minimization for the ground state in all SzS_{z} sectors. Fig. 2(a) and (b) show the final energy and magnetization ⟨𝑺^2⟩\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle in a system with 21 unit cells and 28 particles. For |Sz|≤7​ℏ|S_{z}|\leq 7\,\hbar, the ground state energies are approximately degenerate, and all states reach approximately the total magnetization ⟨S^2⟩=56​ℏ2\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle=56\,\hbar^{2}. This matches the expectation for a ferromagnetic state with total spin S=7​ℏS=7\,\hbar and magnetization ⟨S^2⟩=S⁡(S+1)=56​ℏ2\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle=S(S+1)=56\,\hbar^{2}. Remarkably, the ferromagnetic state is already identified from the calculation at Sz=0S_{z}=0. This demonstrates that the method is sufficiently accurate and expressive to learn the magnetized state even when restricting to the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector. The sectors with Sz>7​ℏS_{z}>7\hbar enforce magnon excitations and the energy difference E⁡(Sz+ℏ)−E⁡(Sz)E(S_{z}+\hbar)-E(S_{z}) for Sz≥7​ℏS_{z}\geq 7\hbar [Fig. 2(a)] measures the magnon excitation energy.

To pin down the nature of the ferromagnetic state, we compute the total occupation ∑α⟨c𝒌,α,σ†​c𝒌,α,σ⟩\sum_{\alpha}\langle c_{\bm{k},\alpha,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k},\alpha,\sigma}\rangle summed over bands α\alpha and resolved by momenta 𝒌\bm{k} within the first Brillouin zone and spin σ\sigma [Fig. 2(c) and (d)]. While the occupation of the dominant spin ↑\uparrow is uniform throughout the Brillouin zone [Fig. 2(c)], the minority spin ↓\downarrow is partially occupied around the center of the Brillouin zone [Fig. 2(d)]. This minimizes the kinetic energy of the minority spin: The occupied momenta have minimal energy in the corresponding band structure shown in Fig. 1(b). The partial filling within a sharp Fermi sea of the minority spin band indicates that the state is metallic. The momentum-space distribution is consistent with Stoner ferromagnetism picture, with spin-imbalanced band occupation due to exchange splitting. Here, the lowest band is fully occupied by the majority-spin electrons and partially occupied by the minority-spin electrons.

Direct evidence of metallic ferromagnetism in WSe2/WS2 has not yet been experimentally observed. Encouragingly, magnetic circular dichroism data [67] shows a Curie-Weiss like temperature dependence, with a positive Weiss constant indicating possible ferromagnetism at filling fractions ν∈[1.2,1.4]\nu\in[1.2,1.4]. This is consistent with our finding of the ferromagnetic ground state at filling fraction ν=4/3\nu=4/3 reported here.

Antiferromagnetism.— In a SU(2)-symmetric system, Néel antiferromagnetism has zero net magnetization ⟨𝑺^2⟩=0\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{2}\rangle=0, instead it exhibits a finite staggered magnetic polarization ⟨𝑺^A−𝑺^B⟩>0\langle\hat{\bm{S}}^{A}-\hat{\bm{S}}^{B}\rangle>0, where 𝑺^A/B\hat{\bm{S}}^{A/B} is the total magnetization of electrons restricted to sublattice regions A/B, which forms a bipartite honeycomb lattice.

We search for antiferromagnetism in moiré semiconductors that naturally realize a long-wavelength honeycomb lattice: twisted transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers where low-energy bands are derived from interlayer hybridized Γ\Gamma-valley states [6, 78]. This class of systems, such as twisted double bilayer WSe2 [22], has typically a large effective mass m∗≈mem^{*}\approx m_{e} and hybridization moiré potential strength of 10 to 20 meV [6, 78]. In the following we use as default parameters the effective mass m∗=mem^{*}=m_{e}, moire potential strength V=15​meVV=15\ {\rm meV}, shape φ=π\varphi=\pi, dielectric constant of the surrounding insulator ϵ=6\epsilon=6, and moire lattice constant aM=6​nma_{\rm M}=6\ {\rm nm} which corresponds to a twist angle of θ=3.00∘\theta=3.00^{\circ} using the typical monolayer lattice constant of 3.15​Å3.15\,\AA.

In this parameter regime, the honeycomb moiré modulation produces narrow minibands with bandwidth of a few tens of meV [Fig. 3(a)], which is comparable to the typical interaction strength e24​π​ϵ​ϵ0​ℓ=76​meV\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon\epsilon_{0}\ell}=76\ {\rm meV}. We consider the filling of two electrons per unit cell, so that in the noninteracting case, the lowest-energy band is fully filled up to the symmetry-enforced Dirac cone at the KK points. In the opposite regime of strong interaction, each sublattice of the honeycomb potential localizes an electron, and kinetic superexchange neighboring A/B sites leads to an antiferromagnetic ordering.

For the realistic material parameters used here, this Néel antiferromagnetic order is discovered in the ground state obtained from the NN-VMC optimization: the real-space spin polarization ⟨n↑​(𝐫)−n↓​(𝐫)⟩\langle n_{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r})-n_{\downarrow}(\mathbf{r})\rangle alternates between the two sublattices [Fig. 3(b)]. To quantify the onset and strength of antiferromagnetism we evaluate the staggered order parameter

Mz=⟨SzA−SzB⟩,M_{z}=\Big\langle S_{z}^{A}-S_{z}^{B}\Big\rangle, (3)

where SzA/BS_{z}^{A/B} denotes the total spin within the two moiré sublattice regions A/B. Figure 3(c) shows MzM_{z} as a function of moiré potential strength VV at fixed interaction strength: increasing VV localizes carriers within the moiré unit cell, reduces the effective bandwidth, and drives a rapid growth of Néel correlations. The sudden jump from Mz=0M_{z}=0 to a finite value at Vc=7.7​meVV_{\rm c}=7.7\ {\rm meV} indicates a correlation-driven transition from a paramagnetic metal into a robust antiferromagnetic state.

Finally, we distinguish an antiferromagnetic insulator from an antiferromagnetic metal by examining the small-qq behavior of the static structure factor [Fig. 3(d)]. Plotting 4​π​S​(q)/q24\pi S(q)/q^{2} highlights the long-wavelength response: an insulating state exhibits a finite q→0q\to 0 limit (incompressible, gapped charge sector) [51], while a divergence as q→0q\to 0 signals a gapless, metallic response [8, 18, 19, 20]. At small V<VcV<V_{\rm c}, the static structure factor indicates a metallic state while for V≫VcV\gg V_{\rm c} the data indicates insulating behavior. This result is consistent with the fact that Néel order parameters opens up an energy gap at the Dirac points.

Discussion.— Our results show that the NN-VMC technique can reliably and autonomously solve magnetic phases that emerge from the interplay of Pauli principle and Coulomb interactions. Because the method operates directly in the continuum and is systematically improvable through the neural network dimensions and optimization effort, it enables quantitatively accurate predictions of magnetism in realistic material models. Importantly, our results demonstrate that the approach autonomously identifies the magnetized state in the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector – eliminating the need to compare calculations from different spin sectors.

More broadly, accurately describing spin effects is essential across chemistry, biophysics, and quantum materials, because key functionalities are often controlled by competing spin states. In chemical reactions, multiple spin-resolved potential-energy surfaces compete and the ground spin state can change during bond stretching – so that the resulting forces are highly sensitive to the spin state during the reaction [58, 25, 33]. As a concrete example, in transition-metal catalysis, multiple spin states can lie close in energy, and changes in the transition-metal spin state can substantially modify activation barriers and selectivity [32, 17]. In drug metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes, substrate binding induces spin shifts in the heme iron, which changes reduction potential and thereby oxygen activation and selectivity [31, 35, 37, 65]. In the cuprate high-temperature superconductors, kinetic superexchange between spins is a key contributor to the Cooper pairing [52]. Since standard electronic-structure methods can struggle precisely in these regimes of strong correlation and competing spin states [38, 71], our ability to solve magnetic ground states from the continuum many-electron problem supports NN-VMC as a promising route toward more predictive simulations in a wide range of spinful systems.

Appendix A Training details

The hyperparameters used for training our model are summarized in Tab. 1.

Our neural network VMC implementation is based on Refs. [57, 73, 27] and our public codebase PeriodicWave [28]. Specific details to our implementation are discussed in Ref. [27].

Our calculations for the ferromagnetic phase (Fig. 2) were performed without a Jastrow factor. For the calculations for the antiferromagnetic phase (Fig. 3), we used a simple Jastrow factor to enforce cusp conditions, as introduced in Ref. [73].

In order to exclude local minima, we performed multiple runs with random initialization. All runs converged to the same magnetic order. This is also illustrated by Fig. 2(a) and (b): All of these runs were performed with random initialization and different SzS_{z}, and all runs converged towards an equivalent ferromagnetic state within that SzS_{z} sector. The antiferromagnetic state performed similarly. We previously benchmarked this approach on similar TMD systems with band-projected exact diagonalization (BPED), where we demonstrated that NNVMC reaches significantly lower energies than BPED by avoiding discretization [27].

Appendix B Finite-size considerations

Because the minority spin in the ferromagnetic state [Fig. 2] partially fills the lowest band, the system size must be chosen carefully in order to avoid frustration of the ferromagnetic state by partial filling of momentum shells of either majority or minority spins. In the chosen six-fold symmetric supercell of 21 unit cells, a filling of 28 electrons allows the minority spin to fully occupy the inner shell of 7 electrons while the majority spin fully fills the band so that frustration of the ferromagnetic state is avoided [this is demonstrated by the spin-resolved occupation numbers in Fig. 2(c) and (d)]. The next promising system size has a C6C_{6}-fold symmetric supercell of 39 unit cells and 52 electrons, so that the minority spin of 13 electrons can fully fill the two inner shells.

The antiferromagnetic state is at filling of two electrons per unit cell which fully fills the lower band. Therefore, any sixfold symmetric periodic supercell can be used to study the antiferromagnetic state.

Appendix C Supplemental numerical data

C.1 Spin density and density-density correlation

We include in Fig. 4 the spin polarization along the SzS_{z} axis of the itinerant ferromagnet, computed in the Sz=0S_{z}=0 sector. Because in this sector, the spin order does not align with the computational spin SzS_{z} basis, the spin polarization along the SzS_{z}-direction in Fig. 4 is close to zero.

We further remark that the spin polarization of the itinerant ferromagnetic state computed for the computational basis aligned with the magnetization, i.e. for Sz=7​ℏS_{z}=7\,\hbar, [Fig. 1(c) in the main text], displays a slightly negative spin density (slightly red regions) at the B (higher-energy) lattice sites of the charge-transfer moire potential.

Figure 5 shows the spin-resolved density-density correlation function for the itinerant ferromagnetic state. The data is consistent with a Fermi liquid ground state.

For completeness, we include in Fig. 6 the spin-resolved density-density correlation function for the antiferromagnetic state at 54 particles.

C.2 Energies

We provide the ground state energies of our final wavefunctions used to generate the results shown in Fig. 2 and 3 in the main text for reproducibility and future benchmark.

In the numerical calculations, we convert SI units to natural units and solve a Hamiltonian of the form

H\displaystyle H =∑i(−12​∇i2+V~​(𝐫i))+12​∑i∑i≠jU|𝐫i−𝐫j|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\tilde{V}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{U}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|}, (4)

where V~(𝐫)=−2V~∑j=13cos⁡(𝐠j⋅𝐫+φ)\tilde{V}(\mathbf{r})=-2\tilde{V}\sum_{j=1}^{3}\cos(\mathbf{g}_j \cdot\mathbf{r} + \varphi). Converting from SI to natural units of Eq. (4), energies are measured in 2​π3​ℏ2m∗​aM2\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m^{*}a_{\rm M}^{2}} and lengths in ℓ=aM/2​π/3=4.31​nm\ell=a_{\rm M}/\sqrt{2\pi/\sqrt{3}}=4.31\ {\rm nm}. In these units, the moire length is set to a~M=2​π/3\tilde{a}_{\rm M}=\sqrt{2\pi/\sqrt{3}} so that the mean interparticle distance equals 1/ν1/\sqrt{\nu} where ν=Nel/Nuc\nu=N_{\rm el}/N_{\rm uc} is the filling fraction defined as the ratio of electron number by number of unit cells in the supercell.

For the itinerant magnet presented in the main text [Fig. 2] with m∗=0.5​mem^{*}=0.5m_{e}, potential strength V=15​meVV=15\ {\rm meV}, dielectric constant ϵ=6\epsilon=6, the energy scale is 2​π3​ℏ2m∗​aM2=8.22​meV\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m^{*}a_{\rm M}^{2}}=8.22\ {\rm meV} and length scale ℓ=aM/2​π/3=4.31​nm\ell=a_{\rm M}/\sqrt{2\pi/\sqrt{3}}=4.31\ {\rm nm}. Converting to natural units, the potential strength is V~=1.82\tilde{V}=1.82 and the interaction strength U=ℓ/aB∗=6.78U=\ell/a_{B}^{*}=6.78 where aB∗=4​π​ϵ​ϵ0​ℏ2e2​m∗=0.635​nma_{B}^{*}=\frac{4\pi\epsilon\epsilon_{0}\hbar^{2}}{e^{2}m^{*}}=0.635\ {\rm nm} is the effective Bohr radius. Table 2 contains the ground state energies and total spin of the data shown in Fig. 2.

For the antiferromagnetic model [Fig. 3], the default parameters are effective mass m∗=mem^{*}=m_{e}, moire potential strength V=15​meVV=15\ {\rm meV}, moire lattice constant aM=6​nma_{\rm M}=6\ {\rm nm}, and dielectric constant of the surrounding insulator ϵ=6\epsilon=6. These translate to natural units V~=2\tilde{V}=2, U=10U=10. The energy scale is 2​π3​ℏ2m∗​aM2=7.68​meV\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m^{*}a_{\rm M}^{2}}=7.68\ {\rm meV}. Table 3 contains the ground state energies of the wavefunctions used to generate the results for the antiferromagnetic model presented in Fig. 3 in the main text.

For accurate comparison for future benchmark, the direct energies in natural units as reported in Tabs. 2 and 3 should be used, not their conversion to meV, in order to avoid rounding errors in the unit conversion.
